q: Canine distemper virus is confirmed in a shelter ferret. What is the appropriate management?
o: Isolate and treat with supportive care; some ferrets recover
Humane euthanasia — CDV is 100% fatal in ferrets — then separate exposed animals and vaccinate all healthy unvaccinated ferrets
Transfer to a specialty hospital for antiviral therapy
Give anti-canine-distemper hyperimmune serum and monitor 4 weeks
e: CDV has a 100% case-fatality rate in ferrets with no successful treatment. Euthanasia minimizes suffering and outbreak risk; vaccinate all healthy unvaccinated in-contact ferrets and separate exposed animals.

q: Twenty minutes after a CDV vaccine at intake, a ferret becomes lethargic with vomiting and collapse. Best first-line treatment?
o: IV antivirals for presumed active CDV
Diphenhydramine 2–4 mg/kg IM/IV and supportive care; epinephrine for severe cases
Oral dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Aural ivermectin for a vestibular crisis
e: Ferrets have a high prevalence of vaccine anaphylaxis, typically within ~25 minutes of CDV or rabies vaccination. Diphenhydramine 2–4 mg/kg IM/IV is first-line; severe cases need epinephrine, dexamethasone and oxygen.

q: A 2-year-old spayed jill develops bilateral symmetrical alopecia starting at the tail base and progressing rostrally, plus vulvar swelling. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Dermatophytosis
Adrenocortical disease
Aleutian disease
Normal seasonal weight fluctuation
e: Tail-base-to-head symmetrical alopecia plus vulvar swelling in a spayed female is classic adrenocortical disease — strongly associated with early-age spay/neuter and almost exclusive to US ferret populations.

q: Why does an unbred jill develop life-threatening anaemia if not spayed?
o: Chronic blood loss from uterine adenocarcinoma
Ferrets are induced ovulators — persistent oestrus causes hyperestrogenism and bone-marrow suppression
Iron deficiency from an all-meat diet
Aleutian-disease-induced haemolysis
e: Ferrets are induced ovulators; an unbred jill stays in oestrus, and chronic hyperestrogenism causes non-regenerative anaemia and bone-marrow suppression. This is a key reason to spay shelter jills.

q: A ferret coronavirus enteritis (ECE) outbreak is suspected. Which statement is correct?
o: A feline coronavirus PCR will reliably detect ferret coronavirus
Feline coronavirus PCR will NOT detect ferret coronavirus; diagnosis needs RT-PCR plus IHC of jejunum/ileum
ECE is uniformly fatal like FRSCV
Older ferrets are protected; only neonates get sick
e: Feline coronavirus PCR does not detect ferret coronavirus. ECE diagnosis requires ferret-specific RT-PCR and IHC of jejunum/ileum, since presence of virus alone isn't confirmatory. Older ferrets get sick after exposure to young asymptomatic carriers.

q: In which US-endemic regions should systemic fungal disease be on the ddx for a ferret with respiratory signs?
o: Blastomyces in the SE/Mississippi-Ohio valleys and Coccidioides in the SW US
Only the Pacific Northwest
Anywhere — these fungi are contagious between ferrets
Only tropical climates
e: Blastomyces dermatitidis is endemic in the SE US and Mississippi/Ohio river valleys; Coccidioides immitis in the SW US. These fungi are NOT contagious between ferrets and are unlikely to arise in a shelter unless the ferret was exposed before entry.

q: A young shelter ferret has chronic mucoid/bloody diarrhoea, thickened intestinal loops and partial rectal prolapse. Which agent — also the cause of hamster wet tail — is most likely?
o: Helicobacter mustelae
Lawsonia intracellularis (proliferative bowel disease)
Clostridium botulinum
Eimeria furonis
e: Lawsonia intracellularis causes proliferative bowel disease in young ferrets and is the same agent behind wet tail in hamsters (and disease in swine and rabbits). Treat with chloramphenicol or metronidazole plus stress reduction.

q: Why is oral (enteral) penicillin contraindicated in rabbits?
o: It is inactivated by rabbit gastric acid
It disrupts the cecal microbiome causing fatal Clostridium overgrowth (enterotoxaemia)
Rabbits are allergic to all beta-lactams
It causes irreversible renal failure
e: Enteral penicillin disrupts the cecal flora and causes fatal Clostridium overgrowth (antibiotic-associated enterotoxaemia). For rabbit syphilis, injectable penicillin G is used; oral penicillin must never be given.

q: Which ectoparasiticide must NOT be used on rabbits?
o: Imidacloprid
Selamectin
Fipronil
Ivermectin
e: Fipronil is contraindicated in rabbits (associated with toxicity/death). Imidacloprid, lufenuron and selamectin are generally safe; ivermectin is used for mites. Dog/cat flea-and-tick collars and insecticide dips must also be avoided.

q: Which statement about RHDV is correct?
o: It is an enveloped virus easily killed by standard QAC alone
It is a reportable, non-enveloped calicivirus; disinfect with 0.5% sodium hypochlorite or 1% formalin
Neonatal rabbits are the most susceptible age group
Absence of blood from the orifices reliably rules it out
e: RHDV is a reportable, non-enveloped calicivirus affecting rabbits >2 months (neonates are resistant). Because it is non-enveloped it resists many disinfectants — use 0.5% sodium hypochlorite or 1% formalin. Lack of orifice bleeding does NOT rule it out.

q: A shelter is 300 miles (483 km) from an area with RHD reported last year; its rabbits are unvaccinated and a new arrival had outdoor exposure 5 days ago. Per the algorithm, what applies?
o: No quarantine — single domestic animals never need it
The rabbit is 'at risk' → 10-day quarantine of the incoming rabbit, plus risk-mitigation
Immediate euthanasia of the incoming rabbit
Vaccinate and place directly into the general population with no quarantine
e: Within 500 miles/800 km of recent RHD, do an individual risk assessment: outdoor exposure in the last 10 days, an unvaccinated general population, or no proof of RHDV2 vaccination each make a rabbit 'at risk' → 10-day quarantine of incoming at-risk rabbits plus risk-mitigation.

q: A dwarf-breed rabbit presents with head tilt and nystagmus. Which is the MOST likely cause, versus a standard-breed rabbit?
o: Pasteurella otitis in both breeds equally
Encephalitozoon cuniculi in the dwarf breed; Pasteurella/otitis is more likely in standard breeds
RHDV in both
Rabbit syphilis
e: In dwarf breeds, vestibular signs (head tilt) are most often caused by E. cuniculi; in standard breeds the cause is more likely Pasteurella multocida or otitis. E. cuniculi is an intracellular microsporidian (a fungus) with seroprevalence 7.5–84.7%.

q: Routine antibiotic choices considered appropriate for rabbits include:
o: Oral penicillin, lincomycin and clindamycin
Doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfa and fluoroquinolones
Amoxicillin and ampicillin
Erythromycin and oral cephalexin
e: Doxycycline, TMS and fluoroquinolones are appropriate in rabbits. Narrow-spectrum oral antibiotics targeting Gram-positives (penicillins, lincomycin, clindamycin) risk fatal dysbiosis/enterotoxaemia.

q: A rabbit's urine is red-orange. Best next step to distinguish porphyrinuria from true hematuria?
o: Abdominal radiographs
Wood's lamp — porphyrins fluoresce while blood does not
Urine culture
Renal biopsy
e: Rabbit urine often contains porphyrins causing red/orange discoloration (intermittent, lasting 3–4 days). A Wood's lamp rapidly differentiates fluorescing porphyrinuria from true hematuria.

q: Why is routine spaying recommended in shelter does by 6–9 months of age?
o: To prevent rabbit syphilis
Because 50–80% of intact does over 3–4 years develop uterine adenocarcinoma
To eliminate Pasteurella carriage
To prevent E. cuniculi shedding
e: Uterine adenocarcinoma develops in 50–80% of intact does over 3–4 years, so ovariectomy/OVH is recommended in all non-breeding does at 6–9 months.

q: Why is vitamin C supplementation essential for guinea pigs?
o: They have an unusually high metabolic demand for it as an antioxidant
They cannot synthesize vitamin C (lack L-gulonolactone oxidase) and develop scurvy without dietary supply
They excrete it rapidly in alkaline urine
It is needed for cecotroph production
e: Guinea pigs lack L-gulonolactone oxidase and cannot make ascorbic acid, so it must come from the diet (guinea-pig-formulated pellets plus vegetables like kale, peppers, oranges). Deficiency causes scurvy.

q: A guinea pig has severe pruritus with scratching so intense it mimics seizures. Skin scrape confirms a mite. Agent and zoonotic status?
o: Psoroptes cuniculi; not zoonotic
Trixacarus caviae; ZOONOTIC — temporarily infects humans
Demodex caviae; no zoonotic risk
Cheyletiella; high zoonotic risk
e: Trixacarus caviae (sarcoptic mite) causes intense pruritus that can be confused with seizure activity and is zoonotic (temporary human skin lesions). Treat ivermectin 0.2–0.4 mg/kg SQ q10–14d ×3 and decontaminate the environment.

q: Which species can asymptomatically carry Bordetella bronchiseptica and infect guinea pigs?
o: Only other guinea pigs
Rabbits, dogs, cats and non-human primates
Only wild birds
Only reptiles
e: Bordetella has a broad host range; rabbits, dogs, cats and non-human primates can be asymptomatic carriers, and sharing airspace can be enough to infect guinea pigs. Prevent exposure of guinea pigs to these species.

q: By 5 years of age, what proportion of guinea pigs develop ovarian cysts, and what is a classic sign?
o: ~10%; pruritus
~76%; bilateral symmetrical truncal alopecia with abdominal distension
~30%; head tilt
~50%; polyuria
e: About 76% of guinea pigs develop ovarian cysts by 5 years. Space-occupying cysts cause decreased fertility, anorexia, abdominal distension and bilateral symmetrical truncal (non-pruritic) alopecia.

q: A guinea-pig coordinator proposes pine shavings as bedding. The correct response is:
o: Pine is the preferred substrate
Pine and cedar are contraindicated (aromatic compounds) — use paper-based bedding or hardwood shavings
Pine is fine; only cedar is a problem
Both are fine if changed weekly
e: Pine and cedar shavings release aromatic compounds causing respiratory and skin disease in guinea pigs and small rodents. Use shredded/recycled paper or hardwood shavings.

q: What is 'wet tail', which hamsters are most affected, and the approximate untreated mortality?
o: Bordetella in adults; 10%
Lawsonia intracellularis proliferative ileitis in weanlings (4–8 wk); ~90%
Rotavirus in neonates; 5%
Helicobacter gastritis in adults; rare mortality
e: Wet tail is Lawsonia intracellularis proliferative ileitis, classically in stressed weanling hamsters (4–8 weeks). Mortality approaches 90%; symptomatic hamsters may die within 48 h. Treat aggressively with fluids, electrolytes, bismuth and empiric antibiotics, or euthanise.

q: A rat has chronic respiratory noise and bronchopneumonia; enrofloxacin + doxycycline help but it relapses when stopped. Most likely agent?
o: Sendai virus — self-limiting
Mycoplasma pulmonis — intracellular, lifelong, incurable; controlled but not eliminated
Streptococcus pneumoniae — cured by a longer course
Bordetella — eliminated by a 4-week course
e: M. pulmonis is the most common major respiratory pathogen of rats — an intracellular bacterium causing lifelong infection. Enrofloxacin + doxycycline controls signs but does not eliminate it; recrudescence on stopping antibiotics is the norm.

q: Which rodent-associated zoonosis is the primary cause of rat-bite fever in humans?
o: Leptospira interrogans
Streptobacillus moniliformis
Yersinia pestis
Bordetella bronchiseptica
e: Streptobacillus moniliformis is the primary cause of rat-bite fever. Wild and pet rats are asymptomatic carriers (nasopharynx/middle ear/respiratory tract; present in urine and blood). Transmission via bites, scratches, excreta or contaminated food/water.

q: Which zoonoses are specifically flagged as risks when handling small rodents at wellness exam?
o: Rabies, FIV and FeLV
Hantavirus, LCMV and Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat-bite fever)
Brucella and Q fever
Toxoplasma and Echinococcus
e: The chapter flags hantavirus, LCMV and S. moniliformis (rat-bite fever) as the zoonotic risks for small rodents. No routine vaccination or diagnostic testing is performed at the wellness exam.

q: Which disinfectants are specifically contraindicated in reptile and amphibian enclosures?
o: Dilute bleach (1:32)
Quaternary ammonium compounds
Phenolic compounds and glutaraldehyde
Accelerated hydrogen peroxide
e: Phenolic compounds and glutaraldehyde are toxic to reptiles and amphibians and must never be used. Dilute bleach (1:32) and QAC are recommended, followed by thorough rinsing because their skin is highly absorptive.

q: Which statement about reptile UVB lighting is correct?
o: UVB can be delivered through glass to reduce burns
UVB (290–320 nm) must not be filtered through glass/acrylic, sits 12–18 inches (30.5–45.7 cm) away, and the bulb is replaced every 12 months
UVB is most important for carnivorous snakes
Output stays constant until the visible light fails
e: UVB (290–320 nm) is essential mainly for herbivorous/omnivorous reptiles to synthesize active vitamin D. It must not pass through glass or acrylic (which block it), should be 12–18 inches (30.5–45.7 cm) from the animal, and the bulb replaced every 12 months because output declines before visible light does.

q: What thermal arrangement do reptiles require in a shelter enclosure?
o: A single uniform temperature throughout
Ambient 80–85 °F (26.7–29.4°C) with a secondary focal heat source ~10 °F (5.6°C) warmer, so the animal can choose its temperature from a gradient
As hot as possible to speed metabolism
Room temperature with no supplemental heat
e: Reptiles thermoregulate behaviourally and need a gradient: ambient 80–85 °F (27–29 °C) plus a focal basking source ~10 °F warmer. Too cold causes immunosuppression and GI stasis; too hot causes thermal burns and acute death.

q: For record-keeping and intake of reptiles in a shelter, which is correct?
o: Group several reptiles under one ID to save records
Individualize ID and records; use temporary non-toxic paint or nail polish; review local ownership laws before accepting
Reptiles are social and should be co-housed for comfort
Cat litter is the preferred substrate
e: Records must be individualized (never group multiple reptiles under one ID); temporary marking uses non-toxic paint or nail polish. Local laws must be reviewed before accepting reptiles, which are non-social and should not be co-housed or kept with carnivorous mammals. Cat litter must never be used.

q: What is the reported prevalence of equine squamous gastric ulcer disease in horses in training/competition versus untrained horses?
o: Under 5% in both groups
17–39% in untrained/unworked horses rising to 66–100% in those in training/competition
Always 100% regardless of work
Higher in untrained horses
e: Squamous gastric ulcer disease affects roughly 17–39% of untrained/unworked horses and 66–100% of horses in training or competition, reflecting the impact of management and intermittent feeding on a trickle-feeding species.

q: Which pathogens are the priority concern during equine intake quarantine (2–3 weeks)?
o: Rabies and West Nile only
EHV (equine herpes myeloencephalopathy), Salmonella and strangles (S. equi)
FeLV and FIV
RHDV and myxomatosis
e: Quarantine runs 2–3 weeks. EHV and Salmonella have large numbers of latently infected shedders stressed by transport, and strangles (Streptococcus equi) is common in the auction/holding facilities rescue horses pass through.

q: An orphan foal follows people like a dog, suckles clothing and initiates rearing/mounting play with humans. What is this and how is it managed?
o: Normal foal play; no intervention needed
Overhandled foal syndrome — limit human interaction, bucket-feed rather than bottle-feed, disassociate humans from mealtime, and provide equine companionship
Colic — refer for surgery
Strangles — isolate and treat
e: Overhandled foal syndrome arises when orphan foals over-bond to humans, producing unsafe behaviour and limited trainability. Management: minimize human interaction, bucket-feed (not bottle), use remote bucket filling to disassociate humans from feeding, and provide equine companionship.

q: A shelter horse paces and weaves in its stall. The correct interpretation/response is:
o: Punish the behaviour to extinguish it
These are locomotor stereotypies — natural responses to physical/psychological discomfort that should not be punished; address the underlying cause and provide turn-out and forage
Confine the horse 24/7 to limit movement
Increase grain meals to provide more energy
e: Pacing, circling, weaving and pawing are locomotor stereotypies reflecting physical or psychological discomfort and should not be punished. Management addresses the underlying cause: continuous forage, turn-out (not 24/7 stalling), and equine company. Cribbing (an oral stereotypy) affects 2–10% of horses.

q: A horse is chewing wood and licking objects. What deficiency does this most suggest?
o: Protein deficiency
Salt/mineral deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency
Taurine deficiency
e: Wood chewing and object licking are signs of salt/mineral deficiency. Horses should have continuous access to an all-forage diet plus salt/trace-mineral licks.

q: Which avian zoonosis is caused by an obligate intracellular bacterium that remains stable in dried droppings for months, making daily feces removal the single best control?
o: Avian mycobacteriosis
Psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci)
Aspergillosis
Newcastle disease
e: Psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci) is an obligate intracellular bacterium stable in dry feces for months; people are infected mainly by inhaling/ingesting dried droppings. Best protection is sanitation (remove feces daily); treat birds with doxycycline for 45 days.

q: A shelter receives a parrot for an avian-friendly disinfection protocol. Which is correct for the bird's respiratory health?
o: Use a strongly scented aerosol disinfectant for thorough coverage
Use an unscented, non-aerosol disinfectant such as dilute bleach; avoid household odours, chemicals, and aerosols
Phenolic compounds are ideal for birds
Glutaraldehyde fogging is recommended
e: Avian respiratory tracts are highly sensitive. Use an unscented, non-aerosol disinfectant (dilute bleach) and avoid household odours, aerosols, and harsh chemicals.

q: Why must intracoelomic (intraperitoneal) fluids be avoided in birds?
o: Birds have no peritoneal cavity
Birds lack a diaphragm and their air sacs connect directly to the lungs, so intracoelomic fluid can drown the bird
It is too painful without anaesthesia
Birds cannot absorb fluid from the coelom
e: Birds lack a diaphragm and their air sacs connect directly with the lungs, so intracoelomic fluids can flow into the pulmonary parenchyma and drown the bird. Give fluids orally, SC, or IO instead.

q: In a psittacine, how should organisms cultured from the droppings be interpreted?
o: Gram-negative organisms are normal flora; gram-positive are pathogens
Gram-positive flora is normal; gram-negative organisms are considered potential pathogens
All bacteria in droppings are abnormal
Only fungi are significant; bacteria are irrelevant
e: In psittacines, normal GI flora is predominantly gram-positive. Gram-negative organisms in the droppings are regarded as potential pathogens. Rare contagious bacterial disease is usually Salmonella, Mycobacterium, or Chlamydophila psittaci.

q: What is the most common fungal disease of psittacines, and what is a key preventive measure?
o: Candidiasis; avoid antibiotics entirely
Aspergillosis; clean daily and avoid corncob and walnut-shell bedding
Cryptococcosis; use UVB lighting
Histoplasmosis; feed only pelleted diets
e: Aspergillosis is the most common fungal disease of psittacines — a ubiquitous, non-contagious soil fungus causing severe respiratory disease via spore inhalation, with high incidence tied to poor management. Prevent with daily cleaning and by avoiding corncob and walnut-shell bedding; immunocompromised raptors/seabirds get prophylactic itraconazole.

q: Under the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act, which birds are EXCEPTIONS that do not require a USFWS permit to possess?
o: Hawks, owls, and eagles
Pigeons, European starlings, English (house) sparrows, and game species
Songbirds and doves
All native waterfowl
e: The Migratory Bird Treaty Act prohibits possessing any part of native migratory birds without a USFWS permit. The exceptions are pigeons, European starlings, English (house) sparrows, and game species (which may still carry state restrictions).

q: A wild raccoon is brought to your clinic. Legally, what may a veterinary hospital do?
o: Provide indefinite long-term care without any permit
Provide emergency care but, in most states, possess it only ~48 hours before transferring to a permitted rehabilitator — and rabies vector species need a special permit
Immediately release it back to where it was found
Keep it as a clinic mascot once healthy
e: A vet may give emergency care, but long-term care requires a state rehabilitator's permit; most states allow possession only up to ~48 hours before transfer. Rabies vector species (like raccoons) require a separate special permit, and relocating RVS for release is illegal in most states.

q: Which group correctly lists the principal rabies vector species relevant to a shelter, plus the one rodent of higher concern?
o: Squirrels, chipmunks, rabbits, and opossums
Raccoons, skunks, foxes, and bats — plus woodchucks (the one rodent group with higher rabies susceptibility)
Mice, rats, gerbils, and hamsters
Deer, horses, and cattle
e: Rabies vector species are raccoons, skunks, foxes, and bats; woodchucks are the one rodent group with notably higher rabies susceptibility. Squirrels, chipmunks, other rodents, rabbits, and opossums rarely have rabies.

q: A staff member without rabies pre-exposure vaccination offers to examine an infant raccoon ('it's just a baby'). The correct response is:
o: Allow it — infants are too young to carry rabies
No one without rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis may handle potential rabies vector species, and age has no bearing on whether the animal carries the virus
Allow it if gloves are worn
Allow it only if the raccoon appears healthy
e: No veterinary staff member may handle wildlife — especially potential rabies vector species — without rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis (a liability mandate). Age has no bearing on whether an animal carries the virus; an infant raccoon can carry rabies. Always use gloves regardless.

q: A caller asks if they can catch rabies from grass a rabid fox drooled on last night. The correct answer is:
o: Yes — dried saliva on surfaces is highly infectious
No — rabies cannot penetrate intact skin and the virus is not viable once saliva dries; it spreads via saliva into bites, fresh cuts/abrasions, or mucous membranes
Yes — rabies is airborne in the environment
Only if the grass is still wet with dew
e: Rabies cannot penetrate intact skin and the virus is not viable after saliva dries. It is transmitted by saliva entering a bite wound, fresh scratch/abrasion, or mucous membrane — not by blood, urine, feces, or the open environment.

q: Which wildlife zoonosis has roundworm eggs that resist common disinfectants, survive in the environment for years, and can only be reliably destroyed by high-heat sterilization?
o: Leptospirosis
Baylisascaris procyonis (raccoon roundworm)
Tularemia
Brucellosis
e: Baylisascaris procyonis eggs are not killed by common disinfectants and survive years — only high-heat sterilization (flame/propane torch, boiling lye water) works. In humans the larvae cause neural larva migrans (blindness, neuro damage, death). Designate cages 'raccoon only,' treat raccoon feces as infective waste, and don't house raccoons on dirt.

q: A fledgling songbird arrives after being caught by a house cat, with no visible wounds. What is the priority?
o: No treatment needed since there are no visible wounds
Start antibiotics (e.g., Clavamox) immediately — cat saliva carries virulent bacteria, including Pasteurella, that cause rapid fatal septicaemia; assume invisible puncture wounds
Release it immediately to reduce stress
Withhold all treatment until a rehabilitator arrives
e: Cat-caught wildlife must be started on antibiotics as soon as possible. Cat saliva carries highly virulent bacteria (including Pasteurella) that quickly cause septicaemia and death in small prey; assume invisible puncture wounds even with no visible injury. Clavamox is the most effective choice for cat bites.

q: An opossum brought in is hissing, drooling, and swaying. What does this most likely indicate?
o: Classic rabies — euthanise and submit for testing
A normal defensive bluff routine; opossums are remarkably rabies-resistant due to their low body temperature
Baylisascaris infection
Distemper
e: Opossums are remarkably resistant to rabies (their low body temperature does not support the virus well). Hissing, drooling, and swaying are part of their bluff/threat routine, not rabies. Standard precautions still apply when handling any wild mammal.

q: Per federal rules for migratory birds, which finding mandates euthanasia (absent special permits)?
o: A bird with a single broken blood feather
A bird that cannot feed itself, perch upright, or ambulate where care won't reverse it; complete blindness; or a wing injury requiring amputation at or above the elbow (humero-ulnar joint)
Any bird that is underweight on intake
A bird with external parasites
e: Federal requirements for migratory birds mandate euthanasia of any bird that cannot feed itself, perch upright, or ambulate where care won't reverse it; any completely blind bird; and any bird needing amputation of a leg, foot, or a wing at or above the elbow (humero-ulnar joint) — unless special permits are granted.
